The insight into the inner life is that a heart truly given to truth does not stay neutral about deceit - it recoils from it, and that recoil is the flip side of its love for what is true.

narratives.narrative: The sense (D101) is deceitful (remiyah), 'Deliver me... from a deceitful tongue.' The type (D102) is disposition. The bearer (D105) is the enemies (inferred). The operation (D106) is 'deceive', and the target (D107) is 'with the tongue' (inferred); the coupling (D112) and locus (D116) note it is paired with the lying lips of the same verse. This must be preserved as distinct from H8267:lying#3 in the same verse (directive 8): 'lying lips' (sheqer) and 'deceitful tongue' (remiyah) name two facets of the same hostile speech - the plain lie and the treacherous guile - which the psalmist bundles together in one plea. Manner (D108) 'none'. Absences: source (D103, present:false) - no upstream cause; seat (D104) 'none' as a flag despite the tongue being the instrument - the deceit is produced by the hostile self, not lodged as an organ's home; intensity (D109), specifier (D110), effect (D111) present:false - unmeasured. Prohibition (D113) absent. The discovery note (D114) reads remiyah as the treacherous speech the psalmist would be freed from. Role (D115) characteristic; locus (D116) internal:ib-state. The inner-being finding: deceit here is the thing prayed against - the interior's response to a treacherous tongue is not retaliation but a cry to God for deliverance. The reading defines the victim's posture: surrounded by guile, the heart appeals upward to be rescued from it.
narratives.story: The pilgrim of this short psalm is worn down by a treacherous tongue and cries out to God to be delivered from it. Alongside 'lying lips' in the same breath, the 'deceitful tongue' names the sly, guileful side of that hostile speech - not just plain lies but cunning treachery. His answer to being surrounded by it is not to fight back or lie in return but to appeal upward, asking God for rescue. The passage does not measure the deceit or trace its origin. The insight into the inner life is that when a person is hemmed in by others' guile, one true response of the heart is to cry out to be delivered - to hand the treachery over to God rather than answer it with more of the same.
narratives.variation_note: This second reading of H7423:deceitful (remiyah) names the 'deceitful tongue' the psalmist begs deliverance from, paired with lying lips (Psa 120:2). It differs from #1 (Psa 78:57), where the word images unreliability - a warped bow that fails its aim - and from #3 (Psa 120:3), where the same deceitful tongue is directly addressed and its judgment weighed. Here deceit is the object of a rescue-cry; at 78 it is a failure of dependability; at 120:3 it is confronted and sentenced.

narratives.narrative: The sense (D101) is lying (sheqer), 'Deliver me... from lying lips.' The type (D102) is disposition. The bearer (D105) is the enemies (inferred). The operation (D106) is 'lie', and the target (D107) is 'against the psalmist' (inferred); the coupling (D112) and locus (D116) note it is paired with the deceitful tongue of the same verse. Distinct from H7423:deceitful#2 above (directive 8): 'lying lips' names the plain falsehood, 'deceitful tongue' the treacherous guile - twin facets of the hostile speech the psalmist prays against. Manner (D108) 'none'. Absences: source (D103, present:false) - no upstream cause; seat (D104) 'none' as a flag despite lips being the instrument - the lie is produced by the hostile self; intensity (D109), specifier (D110), effect (D111) present:false - unmeasured. Prohibition (D113) absent. The discovery note (D114) reads sheqer as the falsehood of the foes from which the psalmist begs deliverance. Role (D115) characteristic; locus (D116) internal:ib-state. The inner-being finding: the lie here is again the object of a deliverance-cry - the interior, harassed by false lips, turns to God. Read beside its twin, the finding preserves the distinction between the bald lie and the crafty treachery, while both drive the same movement: a heart appealing to be freed from surrounding falsehood.
narratives.story: In the same cry the pilgrim asks God to deliver him from 'lying lips.' Bundled with the deceitful tongue beside it, this names the plainer face of the assault - the straightforward falsehoods being told against him. Worn down by lies, he does not scheme or hit back; he simply asks God to rescue him from them. The passage does not measure the lies or explain where they come from. The insight into the inner life is that surrounded by falsehood, the honest heart's instinct here is to appeal upward - to ask for deliverance rather than to trade lie for lie.
narratives.variation_note: This third reading of H8267:lying (sheqer) is the 'lying lips' the psalmist begs deliverance from, paired with the deceitful tongue (Psa 120:2). It differs from #1 (Psa 52:3), where lying is a beloved object preferred over righteous speech, and #2 (Psa 109:2), where it is active assault spoken against the psalmist. Here the lie is prayed against from a posture of appeal; at 52 it is cherished by the tyrant; at 109 it is a weapon in mid-strike.

narratives.narrative: The sense (D101) is deceitful (remiyah), 'What shall be done to you, you deceitful tongue?' The type (D102) is disposition. The bearer (D105) is the deceitful tongue itself (inferred) - the organ addressed as though it were the person. The operation (D106) is 'deceive', and the target (D107) is 'the psalmist' (inferred). Manner (D108) 'none'. The coupling (D112) and locus (D116) note it is paired with the judgment it invites - the verse weighs the recompense due to the tongue ('what shall be given to you, and what more shall be done to you?'). This is the distinct move of this third Psalm-120 reading: where v2 pleads for deliverance FROM the deceitful tongue, v3 turns and ADDRESSES it, weighing its coming judgment. Absences: source (D103, present:false) - no upstream cause; seat (D104) 'none' - whole-person; intensity (D109), specifier (D110), effect (D111) present:false - unmeasured, though the note points to the recompense implied. Prohibition (D113) absent. The discovery note (D114) reads remiyah as the treacherous tongue addressed, its recompense weighed. Role (D115) characteristic; locus (D116) internal:ib-state. The inner-being finding: deceit here is confronted - the interior no longer only cries for rescue but turns to face the treacherous tongue and reckon its judgment. The reading captures the movement from appeal (v2) to confrontation (v3), the heart squaring up to the lie and consigning it to what it deserves.
narratives.story: Having asked God to deliver him from a treacherous tongue, the pilgrim now turns and speaks to it directly: 'What will be done to you, you deceitful tongue?' The mood shifts from pleading to facing it down - he weighs what such a tongue has coming to it. Rather than only asking to escape the lie, he now confronts it and hands it over to judgment. The passage does not measure the deceit or trace its source; it fixes on the reckoning it deserves. The insight into the inner life is that dealing with deceit can move from crying for rescue to squarely facing the falsehood and consigning it to justice - not answering the lie, but naming what it has earned.
narratives.variation_note: This third reading of H7423:deceitful (remiyah) directly addresses the deceitful tongue and weighs its judgment (Psa 120:3), a move from appeal to confrontation. It differs from #2 (Psa 120:2), where the same tongue is the object of a deliverance-cry, and #1 (Psa 78:57), where the word images unreliability as a warped bow. Across the three: unreliability (78), rescue-cry (120:2), and here the confronting of the lie with its recompense (120:3).

narratives.narrative: The sense (D101) is vain (shav), 'unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labour in vain.' The type (D102) is state - a condition of futility, not a lie. The bearer (D105) is the builders (inferred). The operation (D106) is 'labour in vain', and the target (D107) is 'without God's building' (inferred) - the movement is human effort spent apart from God and coming to nothing. Manner (D108) 'none'. The coupling (D112) and locus (D116) note it is paired with the watchman's vain vigil (the parallel clause, reading #3). Absences: source (D103, present:false) - no upstream cause named for the futility; seat (D104) 'none' - whole-person; intensity (D109), specifier (D110), effect (D111) present:false - unmeasured. Prohibition (D113) absent. The discovery note (D114) reads shav as human building without God being effort spent on nothing, the work undone before it stands. Role (D115) characteristic. The inner-being finding: 'vain' here is the emptiness of self-reliant labour - the interior that builds without God builds nothing. Within the family this is falsehood/emptiness applied to work: not a lie spoken but a futility lived, the false confidence that human effort alone can raise something lasting.
narratives.story: This psalm opens with a hard truth about human effort: 'unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labour for nothing.' The 'vanity' here is not a lie but futility - work poured out that comes to nothing because God is not in it, a house undone before it even stands. The builders sweat and stack and it all amounts to emptiness apart from him. The passage does not measure the futility or explain its cause; it just states it flatly. The insight into the inner life is that self-reliant effort carries a hidden emptiness: to build a life on your own strength, leaving God out, is to labour hard for nothing.
narratives.variation_note: Of the four H7723:vain (shav) readings, this one is the futility of the builders' labour without God (Psa 127:1a). It differs from #1 (Psa 108:12), where 'vain' is the heart's judgement that human help is empty (a disposition of trust); and from its own passage-mates #3 (the watchman's vain vigil, 127:1b) and #4 (the toiler's anxious labour, 127:2). The three Psalm 127 readings share the theme of empty effort but distinguish the actor - builder, watchman, toiler - preserving each futile labour as its own finding.

narratives.narrative: The sense (D101) is vain (shav), 'unless the Lord watches over the city, the watchman stays awake in vain.' The type (D102) is state. The bearer (D105) is the watchman (inferred). The operation (D106) is 'keep watch in vain', and the target (D107) is 'without God's keeping' (inferred) - vigilance spent apart from God and coming to nothing. Manner (D108) 'none'. The coupling (D112) and locus (D116) note it is paired with the builders' vain toil (the parallel clause, reading #2). This is preserved as distinct (directive 8): the builder's futile labour and the watchman's futile vigil are two images, not one - construction and protection both shown empty without God. Absences: source (D103, present:false) - no upstream cause; seat (D104) 'none' - whole-person; intensity (D109), specifier (D110), effect (D111) present:false - unmeasured. Prohibition (D113) absent. The discovery note (D114) reads shav as the futility of the vigil: the guard's wakefulness is useless if God does not keep the city. Role (D115) characteristic. The inner-being finding: 'vain' here is the emptiness of self-reliant vigilance - staying awake, guarding, straining to protect, all fruitless if God does not keep the city. The interior's anxious watchfulness cannot secure what only God secures; the sleepless effort is spent on nothing.
narratives.story: The psalm's second picture is the night watchman: unless the Lord guards the city, the guard stays awake for nothing. Like the builder's labour, his sleepless vigilance is empty without God - all that straining to keep watch protects nothing if God is not the one keeping it. It is a different image from the builder but the same lesson: effort to protect, just like effort to build, comes to nothing on its own. The passage does not measure the futility or trace its cause. The insight into the inner life is that anxious self-reliance in guarding what we love is just as empty as self-reliant work - the heart that stays awake trying to secure everything by itself is watching in vain.
narratives.variation_note: Of the four H7723:vain (shav) readings, this is the futility of the watchman's vigil without God (Psa 127:1b). It differs from #2 (the builders' vain labour, 127:1a) and #4 (the anxious toiler, 127:2) by the actor and image - guarding rather than building or toiling - and from #1 (Psa 108:12), where 'vain' is the heart's trust-judgement that human help is empty. narratives.story: The psalm's third picture goes straight to the heart: it is pointless to rise before dawn and stay up late, gnawing on 'the bread of anxious toil.' Here the emptiness is not only in the work but in the worry that drives it - the frantic overworking of someone trying to secure life by sheer effort. And it is set against something gentler: God gives sleep to those he loves. What the anxious person grinds themselves down chasing, God simply gives to the trusting as they rest. The passage does not measure the futility, but names the anxiety underneath it. The insight into the inner life is that worried, self-driven striving is empty - the restless heart wears itself out for nothing, while the heart at peace receives from God, in its sleep, what all that anxiety could never earn.
narratives.variation_note: Of the four H7723:vain (shav) readings, this one alone locates the futility in anxious toil - the worry-driven overworking answered by God's gift of sleep to his beloved (Psa 127:2). It differs from #2 (builders) and #3 (watchman), which image empty labour and vigilance, and from #1 (Psa 108:12), the heart's judgement that human help is vain. Here the emptiness reaches furthest inward, into the anxiety behind the effort, making this the most interior of the 'vain' findings.
